ping-pong.note: Uncountable; the official name is "table tennis."

foie gras.note: Uncountable: some foie gras (not "a foie gras").

anti-aging.note: More often used as an adjective: "anti-aging cream."
ex: My mom buys anti-aging cream at the pharmacy.
Does this anti-aging cream really work on wrinkles?
The clinic offers anti-aging treatments for the face.
Sleep and sunscreen are the best tips for anti-aging.

pro-choice.note: Supporting a woman's right to choose abortion; the opposite is "pro-life."
ex: My aunt has always been pro-choice about abortion.
Pro-choice groups held a big rally downtown today.
He voted for the pro-choice candidate in the election.
Are most young voters in your country pro-choice?
Estrogen is an important hormone in the female body.
Her estrogen levels dropped after menopause.
The doctor prescribed estrogen pills for her symptoms.
Estrogen helps keep women's bones strong and healthy.

polka.note: Also in "polka dots": round spots on fabric, like on a dress.

boogie.note: Most often a verb meaning to dance: "Let's boogie!"

sumo.note: Uncountable: watch sumo. A fighter is a "sumo wrestler."

sakura.note: Used mostly about Japan; the usual English name is "cherry blossom."

tsar.note: Also spelled "czar"; in US news it can mean a top official, like "drug czar".
ex: The museum has a portrait of a Russian tsar.
The tsar lived in a huge palace with his family.
People in the village feared the power of the tsar.
Our history lesson today was about the Russian tsars.

leverage.note: Most often "leverage" means power to influence: "We have no leverage over them."
ex: The company used leverage to buy more property.
High leverage makes an investment much more risky.
The bank wants to reduce its leverage this year.
Leverage can increase your profits, but also your losses.
I had a croissant and coffee for breakfast.
This bakery sells fresh croissants every morning.
Can I get a chocolate croissant, please?
The croissant was still warm and soft.
Ecuador is a country right on the equator.
It is hot all year near the equator.
Our ship crossed the equator on the third day.
The equator divides the earth into two halves.
What does this acronym in the email stand for?
My new company uses too many acronyms.
An acronym is a word made from first letters.
Please write the full name, not just the acronym.

pensioner.note: Mostly British; Americans usually say "retiree" or "senior."

ex: The English translation lost some of the nuance.
She explained the small nuances of the new contract.
His paintings are simple but full of nuance.
You need to understand the cultural nuances here.
The dentist gave me a local anesthetic before the filling.
The anesthetic made my mouth numb for hours.
Doctors use a general anesthetic for this surgery.
The anesthetic wore off after a few hours.

header.note: In soccer, a "header" is hitting the ball with your head.

ex: She wore a warm cardigan over her dress.
Please button your cardigan, because it is cold outside.
He has a gray wool cardigan for work.
I bought a new cardigan for the fall.

influenza.note: Formal; in everyday speech people say "flu".

telecom.note: Short for "telecommunications"; often used before another noun.

ex: She smiled at the waiter and said, "Merci."
He jokingly says merci instead of thank you.
Merci for the coffee, that was very kind!
My friend learned to say merci in Paris.
The polio vaccine has saved millions of children.
My grandfather had polio when he was a child.
Polio can cause serious problems with the legs.
Do children in your country still get polio shots?

mackerel.note: Plural is usually "mackerel," the same as the singular.

MILF.note: Vulgar slang; avoid it in polite conversation.

marketplace.note: Often means the market in general: "competition in the global marketplace."
ex: I sold my old bike on an online marketplace.
This marketplace has thousands of sellers from many countries.
She buys handmade gifts on an online marketplace.
Is it safe to buy phones on this marketplace?
